summary: Defines an SDP cryptographic attribute for unicast media streams. The attribute carries a cryptographic key and other parameters to configure security for the stream in a single message or one round trip, and can be used with various transport protocols. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: The call's info card gets a line that hands over the secret key and lock settings, so both sides can scramble their audio the same way.

questions: what is the sdp crypto attribute
how does srtp key exchange work in sdp
subtitle: How to put the secret key for an encrypted call into the call description itself, so both sides can set up SRTP in one round trip.

tldr.problem: SDP describes media streams but has no way to configure SRTP beyond defaults, so two endpoints cannot agree on keys and cipher settings for a secure call.
tldr.mechanism: A new media-level SDP attribute, a=crypto, carries a tag, a crypto-suite name, inline key material and optional session parameters. In offer/answer, each side sends the key it will use for its own outgoing media.
tldr.outcome: It works only when the SDP message itself is authenticated and encrypted, because the master key travels inside it. It is not a key management protocol.

today: RFC 4568 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its sibling approach, which keeps key material apart from the signaling, is covered in RFC 4567.

sections.title: Why SDP Needs a Crypto Attribute
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes multimedia sessions. The Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP, RFC 3711) protects RTP media and is signaled by a secure transport such as RTP/SAVP in the m= line. SDP itself has no means to configure SRTP beyond default values.

RFC 4568 adds a media-level attribute called crypto to signal and negotiate cryptographic parameters. The definition is limited to two-party unicast streams where each source has a unique key. It is defined generically, so other secure transports could use it, but this document defines the details for SRTP only.

SDP was not designed to provide authenticated key establishment, and this specification adds none. It is no replacement for a key management protocol. It suits restricted cases where IPsec, TLS or another protocol, such as SIP S/MIME, protects the whole SDP message.
sections.eli5: A call description lists what is being sent but not how to lock it. This adds a line that says how to lock it and gives the key, so it only makes sense if the whole card travels in a locked envelope.

sections.title: The crypto Attribute
sections.content:
The attribute appears only at the media level, never the session level, and has this form: a=crypto:<tag> <crypto-suite> <key-params> [<session-params>]. Values are case-insensitive unless noted, but the attribute name itself is case-sensitive.

  • The tag is a decimal number with no leading zeroes, unique among the crypto attributes of a media line. In offer/answer it tells the offerer which attribute the answerer chose.
  • The crypto-suite names the encryption and authentication algorithms. Each transport has its own namespace of suites.
  • The key-params field is a key method, a colon, then key information. Only the inline method is defined, meaning the key material is in the attribute itself. When several keys are given, a receiver MUST be able to tell which key a packet uses by inspecting it; trial and error is forbidden.
  • The optional session-params are transport-specific strings. They are either negotiated (apply to both directions) or declarative (apply only to media sent by the party that wrote the SDP).
sections.eli5: The line is like a recipe card: a number to name it, the kind of lock, the key itself, and some extra settings. Each part has a job.

sections.title: Offer/Answer Rules
sections.content:
In the offer/answer model of RFC 3264, the offerer includes one or more crypto attributes per secure media stream, each with a unique tag. The order matters: the most preferred comes first, and a preferred suite SHOULD be cryptographically stronger than a less preferred one.

The suite applies in both directions, but the keys do not. Each endpoint determines its own transmission keys and sends them in SDP to the other side. The answerer MUST accept exactly one offered crypto attribute or reject the stream. Its answer repeats the tag and suite and adds the key or keys it will use for media it sends. The offerer then checks that one of its offered suites and tag came back and that the answer carries keys. If any check fails, the negotiation MUST fail.

A caveat is that media may arrive before the answer, so the offerer cannot yet decrypt it. The RFC suggests a mechanism outside its scope, such as a security precondition in SIP, if clipping is unacceptable.

Outside offer/answer, the sender MUST include exactly one crypto attribute and the receiver either accepts it or SHOULD NOT receive the stream. For SRTP, use outside offer/answer is not defined. If the answerer ignores the unknown attribute but accepts the stream, the offerer sees a crypto-less answer and the negotiation MUST be deemed failed.
sections.eli5: You hand over a list of lock kinds, best first. The other side picks one and sends back its own key. You each lock your own messages with your own key.

sections.title: SRTP Keys, Suites and Session Parameters
sections.content:
An SRTP inline key has the form inline:<key||salt>[|lifetime][|MKI:length]. The master key and salt are concatenated and base64 encoded. Each master key MUST be cryptographically random and unique across the whole SDP message. The optional lifetime is the maximum number of SRTP or SRTCP packets for that key and may be written as a power of two with 2^. The optional MKI (master key identifier) and its length in bytes let a receiver pick among several keys. An MKI length above 128 makes the attribute invalid, and if several keys are given all MUST carry an MKI of the same length. The From/To lifetime form of SRTP is not supported.

Three crypto-suites are defined: AES_CM_128_HMAC_SHA1_80, AES_CM_128_HMAC_SHA1_32 and F8_128_HMAC_SHA1_80. They share a 128-bit master key and a 112-bit master salt, so the decoded key and salt MUST be 30 octets (240 bits) or the attribute is invalid. They differ in cipher (AES counter mode or AES F8) and SRTP authentication tag length (80 or 32 bits).

Session parameters can override SRTP defaults: KDR (key derivation rate), UNENCRYPTED_SRTP, UNENCRYPTED_SRTCP, UNAUTHENTICATED_SRTP (NOT RECOMMENDED), FEC_ORDER, FEC_KEY and WSH (a window size hint the receiver MAY ignore). New parameters are mandatory by default; one starting with a dash is optional. An unknown parameter without a dash makes the attribute invalid.
sections.eli5: The key is a long secret string, plus a note on how long it may be used and a label so you can tell keys apart. A few switches can turn off scrambling or checking, but that is a bad idea.

sections.title: Crypto Contexts, Rekeying and Forking
sections.content:
SRTP needs an SSRC, a roll-over counter (ROC) and a sequence number. The RFC avoids signaling them. The ROC MUST be zero when each SSRC starts sending, and the initial sequence number SHOULD be within 0..2^15-1 to avoid ambiguity if early packets are lost. With late binding, which is RECOMMENDED, the receiver learns the SSRC from the first arriving packet. The context starts as a wildcard on address and port and is instantiated only if the packet authenticates. Context removal follows the same rules as SSRC removal in RTP, so quiet participants MUST send SRTCP at regular intervals.

When a session is modified, any negotiated aspect, such as the suite or master key, can change. If either side's IP address or port changes, it MUST include a new master key, which creates a new context with ROC zero. If a new offer is rejected, the old parameters stay. The answer's keys MUST differ from the offer's, and a receiver MUST NOT reuse the key it received for its own outgoing packets.

Multicast and multipoint streams are not supported. With SIP forking, one offer can draw several answers, which the RFC says breaks the model. It sketches turning each extra answer into a separate two-party exchange but says that is not normative.
sections.eli5: Each side keeps its own counter for its own messages, starting at zero. If someone moves to a new address, they must hand over a fresh key, because nobody can be sure the old counters moved with them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the master key is inside the SDP, the protection of the SDP message decides everything. The RFC says it is REQUIRED that the encapsulating protocol provide strong message authentication, payload encryption and effective replay protection. Encryption is REQUIRED whenever an inline master key appears. Failing to encrypt such an SDP message renders SRTP useless in practically all circumstances. An attacker who can alter an unauthenticated offer might, for example, set an unencrypted parameter and leave an answerer sending unprotected media.

S/MIME and PGP/MIME lack replay protection and need it added. If intermediaries such as SIP proxies inspect the SDP, hop-by-hop protection such as TLS or IPsec SHOULD NOT be used for the crypto attributes, and end-to-end MIME secure multiparts are RECOMMENDED.

On the media side, SRTP integrity mechanisms SHOULD be used. The key-uniqueness rules prevent keystream reuse, which is the main danger when SSRCs collide while a key is shared.
sections.eli5: The key travels inside the message, so the message needs a strong lock of its own. A secret in a see-through envelope is no secret at all.

sections.title: Grammar and IANA Registries
sections.content: The RFC gives ABNF grammars for the generic attribute and the SRTP form, and IANA registered the crypto attribute as media-level. IANA also created an SDP Security Descriptions registry with subregistries for key methods and for media stream transports. The initial key method is inline, and SRTP is the first transport, with its own registries for crypto suites and session parameters. New entries need a Standards Action RFC.
sections.eli5: There is an official list where new lock kinds and settings must be written down, so everyone uses the same names.
